title: A Well for the House
premise: Silas Sandoval has spent her career listening to the dying count backwards from numbers they shouldn't know, and she has written every one down in a ledger she treats as scripture. When her mother's hospice care brings her back to the house where she grew up, the imaginary friend who vanished when Silas was nine is waiting on the porch, unchanged, and the old well in the backyard is beginning to refill. The counting isn't random: it's a countdown to the well's completion, and everyone in the family is on its list. To save them, Silas must abandon the invisibility that kept her safe as a child, confront what she was promised in exchange for her silence, and get the family out ahead of the count before the well refills—even if it means becoming the last name on the list herself.
about_author: Orsen Thornbury is the pen name of a former rural hospice volunteer who spent six years collecting the last words of the dying across three counties. A Well for the House is his second novel, following the quietly acclaimed The Long Corridor.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Last Numbers
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Introduces her habit of recording the backward counts of dying patients, framed as devotion rather than obsession. Her latest patient counts down from 44 and dies smiling. Emotional beat: the comfort of ritual, undercut by the reader's first hint that the numbers mean something.

chapters.title: Notice of Transfer
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She's assigned to a private client in Halloway County—her childhood home, where her mother Marisol now lives alone. Silas hasn't returned in twenty years. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professionalism; she packs the ledger without admitting why.

chapters.title: The Porch
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Arriving at the house, she finds Wren—her imaginary friend from age four to nine—sitting on the porch steps, exactly as remembered, unaged. Wren greets her by name and says, 'You're early.' Emotional beat: vertigo; the past refusing to stay past.

chapters.title: Marisol's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Sharp, lucid, and furious that Silas came. She refuses to discuss the well, which the county capped decades ago after the Alderman boy went down it. That night Marisol catches herself counting under her breath. Emotional beat: a mother's love expressed as eviction.

chapters.title: What the Well Was For
chapters.summary: Silas's POV with interpolated ledger entries. She researches the house's history: three generations of Sandovals, each generation losing one child 'to the water,' each survivor prosperous afterward. Emotional beat: the sickening arithmetic of inherited advantage.

chapters.title: Wren Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Wren reappears inside the house at night, playing the games they played as children but answering every question about the well with riddles. He only says the count started again when Silas crossed the property line. Emotional beat: nostalgia curdling into manipulation.

chapters.title: Forty-Three
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol begins hearing counting through the floorboards. Her memory of Silas's childhood fractures—she can't recall why Silas stopped speaking for a year at age nine. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing like something rising in water.

chapters.title: The Family Arrives
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Brother Teo arrives with his wife Priya and daughter Ana for Marisol's birthday, drawn by an invitation none of them sent. The house feels glad. Emotional beat: warmth with a trapdoor under it—the family together for the first time in years.

chapters.title: Ana Draws the Well
chapters.summary: Ana's POV (close third). Seven-year-old Ana draws pictures of a man made of rope and river who tells her secrets. She knows things about the house she couldn't know. Emotional beat: innocence as a conduit; Silas recognizes her own childhood in it.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas compares her ledger against county records and church registries: every death matches a number, and the intervals are shrinking. The current count began at forty-four—the same number as her patient's. Emotional beat: faith in evidence becoming terror of what the evidence proves.

chapters.title: Teo's Bargain
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo, drowning in debt, finds his grandfather's papers showing the family fortune came with obligations. He starts leaving offerings at the wellhead—a coin, then a photograph, then blood on a dare he doesn't remember making. Emotional beat: need dressed up as curiosity.

chapters.title: Thirty-One
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finally tells Silas part of the truth: at nine, Silas was chosen, and Marisol bargained her out of it by promising 'the next one who belongs.' She has spent twenty years believing she bought time, not a reprieve. Emotional beat: confession as betrayal; loyalty and truth pulling apart.

chapters.title: The Rope-and-River Man
chapters.summary: Ana's POV. Ana meets the figure at the wellhead, who shows her a version of the family where everyone is happy and no one ever left. He asks her to bring him 'the one who writes.' Emotional beat: seduction of belonging; the horror of being wanted.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas realizes her lifelong invisibility—socially, professionally, even in her own family—wasn't temperament but terms: staying unseen kept her off the list. Being noticed by Wren means the terms have lapsed. Emotional beat: rage at a lifetime of smallness that was actually survival.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided. The counting becomes audible to everyone. Teo defends the well ('it's ours, it's always been ours'); Priya finds his offerings and understands what he's traded. Emotional beat: the family fracturing along the fault line of what each will pay.

chapters.title: Wren's True Name
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas forces the confrontation: Wren was never imaginary—he was the previous taken child, the Alderman boy, reshaped into something the well uses as a lure. His 'friendship' was his own corrupted loyalty, keeping children coming so he wouldn't be alone. Emotional beat: pity and fury entwined; power corrupting even its victims.

chapters.title: Evacuation
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya organizes the escape—cars, documents, Marisol refusing to leave. The roads loop back to the house no matter which way they drive. Ana calmly explains that you can't leave during a count. Emotional beat: panic meeting the uncanny; maternal ferocity against geography itself.

chapters.title: Fifteen
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol attempts to renegotiate the bargain, offering herself in place of everyone. The well accepts—but reveals the price was never substitution, only witness: someone must watch the refilling and remember. Emotional beat: sacrifice reframed as sentence.

chapters.title: The Refilling
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Climax begins. The well rises overnight, water climbing the yard, the house groaning on its foundations. Silas reads her ledger aloud at the wellhead—not prayer now, but testimony, naming every taken child. The count stutters. Emotional beat: defiance; documentation weaponized.

chapters.title: Seven
chapters.summary: Climax. Silas's POV with Ana interludes. Silas offers the only trade the well cannot refuse: a keeper who comes willingly and remembers everything—herself—in exchange for the family walking out ahead of the final count. Wren, moved by being named and mourned, breaks his function and holds the water back long enough. Emotional beat: self-erasure as the ultimate act of identity.

chapters.title: Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The family drives out at dawn on a road that finally goes somewhere. Behind them the house stands empty around a full, still well. Ana waves at something on the porch that only she can see, and it waves back once, sadly. Emotional beat: grief and deliverance in the same breath.

chapters.title: One
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Silas's POV. Silas keeps the ledger from inside, writing down the names of the dying across three counties, hearing their counts and answering them with names until each reaches one. On the porch sits a new arrival someday soon—but Silas has changed the terms: no one is taken anymore, only accompanied. Final beat: power accepted, corruptions resisted, truth kept where loyalty failed.
